newsitem.title: PERU: Peru holds new round of talks with Marxist rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru holds new round of talks with Marxist rebels.

text.p: Peru held a new round of talks with Marxist rebels holding 72 VIP hostages in the besieged Japanese ambassador's home on Thursday to try to reach a bloodless end to the 65-day crisis.

A white Red Cross car drove a Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) spokesman -- believed to be second-in-command Rolly Rojas -- to a safe house where government negotiator Domingo Palermo was waiting.
As the car covered the short distance from the diplomatic compound, the MRTA rebels sang a revolutionary anthem commemorating fallen comrades and shouted defiant slogans.
"On the 65th day of the takeover of the residence, no one gives up, damn it," the rebels shouted in unison.
"What is the objective of this mission?" shouted a rebel believed to be MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa through a megaphone. "To free our prisoners," replied other guerrillas.

The roughly 15 MRTA rebels' demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades is the main sticking point with the government, which insists it will not consider this although it is prepared to let the hostage-takers seek asylum abroad.
The two sides held three rounds of talks last week. But the last meeting between Palermo and Rojas on Saturday apparently produced nothing but a commitment to meet again.
Last week's talks prompted speculation the MRTA might be prepared to shift its position on the prisoners' issue.

And in an interview with Reuters at a secret jungle location in eastern Peru this week, the MRTA admitted publicly for the first time it probably would not win its central demand that all jailed comrades be freed.

"I do not think all of the 400-plus (prisoners) are going to get out," said a man who identified himself as Comrade Alejandro, a member of the MRTA's top policy-making body. He said the MRTA was prepared to negotiate how many would be freed depending on their experience and importance in the movement.
But the jungle commander said he doubted Cerpa would ever drop completely the demand for the release of jailed rebels.

Also present at Thursday's new round of talks were members of a "guarantor" commission overseeing negotiations -- Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent and the Vatican's representative, Roman Catholic bishop Juan Luis Cipriani. Japanese government observer Terusuke Terada also attended.

A metal detector was used to make sure nobody entered the Red Cross-supervised safe house with weapons, and cables laid to the embassy residence were believed to give Rojas a direct phone line with Cerpa.

The MRTA stormed the residence on Dec. 17, initially taking more than 500 cocktail party guests hostage. But it released most in the early days of the crisis, holding only those it considered most valuable. The remaining captives, mainly middle-aged and increasingly ailing, include Fujimori's younger brother, two government ministers, top security force and judiciary officials, two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, and the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia.

The rebels insisted on Thursday that no more hostages would be freed on medical grounds, claiming they could get adequate treatment inside the residence. "Any illness is the product of negotiations dragging on," added a statement issued over the Internet on behalf of the MRTA's high command.
Despite more sophisticated medical attention in the last few weeks, concern for the hostages' health has grown as they show increasing signs of stress.

Enriqueta de Mendoza appealed to the MRTA to release her husband, Energy and Mines Vice Minister Juan Mendoza, who has a hernia. "He has the medical report. I do not know what Mr. Cerpa is waiting for," she said outside the residence.
Other hostages required close monitoring for cancer, heart problems and arthritis. The last two hostages released from the compound were freed on medical grounds in January.
